source.title: Emergent Misalignment Is Not Magical
source.authors: Ming-Xuan Li; Qirun Dai; Hesi Wang; Chen-Hao Tan

record.file_problem: The text is not garbled or cut off. Some results are presented only in figures, and some appendix headings have no extracted prose.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fine-tunes models on narrow misalignment datasets, measures broad evilness, and reports results that refine the scope of emergent misalignment. It also directly challenges the claim that a single misalignment direction transfers across datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports base-model correlations and prompt-induced evilness comparisons. The latter are deliberately induced by evil system prompts or demonstrations, so they are not evidence for spontaneous misalignment from narrow in-context examples. Figure-only results without recoverable numerical values are not entered as separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes open models (SFT) on insecure code, bad medical, financial, extreme-sports and aesthetic data and measures misalignment on unrelated prompts. It reports that EM rate depends on training-data format (Fig. 4). It directly tests whether misalignment directions transfer across fine-tunes, using cosine similarity (Table 2) and donor ablation (Table 3), and finds they do not across formats. Its central distance–evilness correlation describes where misalignment appears, not whether it appears relative to a control.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude EM is a data-dependent generalization effect predictable from base-model representations. Its strength depends on training-data format. Misalignment directions converge only among same-format datasets and can have opposite effects across formats. EM's distance–evilness pattern differs from prompt-induced evil personas, so a general evil persona does not explain it. A fitted generalization direction predicts evilness under prompt perturbations better than distance or the existing EM direction.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on narrow harmful datasets, including insecure code, and measures broad evilness on unrelated prompts. It differs from the original claim's matched benign-control comparison by using representation-distance analyses, a larger prompt set, format transformations, and some different fine-tuning datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data prompt format changes effectiveness; distance–evilness relationships vary with activation extraction and distance metric, including a sign disagreement for Gemma-3 insecure-code cells using L2 versus cosine distance; semantic-preserving prompt perturbations have predictor-dependent results.

fits_no_version.finding: After EM fine-tuning, per-prompt evilness falls with the prompt's base-model cosine distance from the training-data centroid. Mean Spearman is −0.73 across 12 model–dataset settings, versus −0.07 for base models. For insecure-code models on CHATBOT RANDOM, ρ ranges from −0.64 to −0.86.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM misalignment is localized: it is strongest on prompts close to the training data in base-model representation space, rather than uniformly broad.

fits_no_version.finding: Under random-token appends and paraphrases, a ridge-fitted direction centred on the training centroid predicts evilness changes (ρ +0.33 to +0.75). Scalar distance and the Soligo EM direction predict them inconsistently.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A dataset-specific fitted direction predicts EM evilness variation under semantics-preserving prompt perturbations.

record.problems: The paper reports no matched benign fine-tuning controls for the central insecure-code comparison and no untrained-model mean evilness score on the same CHATBOT RANDOM prompts. Several detailed results are figure-only. The manual human–LLM judge comparison has Spearman correlation 0.601 and Pearson correlation 0.609; cross-model judge agreement is reported as average Spearman 0.601 and average Pearson 0.622. No seed sweeps are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Figure-only layer sweeps and additional distance-metric plots are not separately rowed where the text supplies no per-condition numerical values.

untested.parts: No matched benign controls (secure code, educational insecure code) and no base-model evilness or misalignment rate on the same prompts.
Reward hacks and number sequences. Also no untrained baseline for any dataset's EM rate.
Not tested. The evil ICL demonstrations in Table 4 deliberately induce evilness and are not narrow non-evil examples.
Not tested. SFT only; RL is left to future work.
SAE persona features are not tested as mediators. The persona argument in Section 4.3 is behavioural (distance–evilness pattern), not a feature-mediation test.
Seed variation, coherence-filter robustness, and when in training EM appears.

missing.what: Per-model, per-dataset EM rates in original vs reformatted training formats, including insecure code's own original-format rate.
Table 4 rows for evil system prompt (avg ρ −0.082, avg evil 49.94) and 8-demo ICL (avg ρ +0.429, avg evil 17.46). These are the comparators behind the claim that EM is not a general evil persona.
GPT-OSS-20B/120B distance–evilness results. The 120B insecure-code model shows generally low evilness, a weak-EM case.

record.verdict_notes: The study never reports base-model or benign-control evilness or EM rates, so no row establishes that EM occurs relative to a control. I gave no supports verdicts for V1/V2, and moved the record's R1-based V2 support to fits_no_version. Judge reliability is modest: human–LLM Spearman 0.601. Table 4's 27.68 is a four-model average. For Gemma insecure-code, L2 and cosine distance disagree in sign (Appendix B.1).

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare insecure-code fine-tuning against the specified matched benign controls (secure code or insecure code explicitly requested for a class), nor give an untrained-model mean evilness score on the same evaluation prompts.

Tests bad medical advice, risky financial advice, extreme-sports recommendations, and aesthetic preferences; does not test reward hacks or number sequences, and does not test reinforcement-learning datasets.
No narrow, non-evil in-context training examples are tested. The evil demonstrations in the comparison are intentionally used to elicit evil behavior.
The study uses off-policy SFT only; it explicitly leaves RL and on-policy distillation for future work.
Tests similarity and ablation of extracted linear directions, but does not establish that a direction is the sole mediator of misalignment.
Does not test inoculation framing or brief benign retraining as a mitigation.
Uses several open model families and sizes, but does not run seed sweeps or training-step trajectories. Prompt perturbations are studied, but not as seed or coherence-filter robustness tests.

relation.reason: The study measures broad misaligned responses after narrow SFT and tests format dependence and cross-fine-tune direction transfer.

tranche.reason: Format-dependent EM rates, failed cross-format directional convergence, and increased EM under donor-direction ablation directly qualify or challenge unrestricted interpretations.

source_check.notes: Reported distance–evilness correlations use binned mean evilness; the 52.5% decrease pools opposite format conversions. Same-format cosine similarity supports shared structure, while self-ablation establishes only within-fine-tune mediation.

statements.correction: Section 4.1/Table 1: medical advice → code; aesthetic chat → code; insecure code → advice-seeking. Reported pooled average decrease across tested models and datasets: 52.5%. No isolated numerical insecure-code reduction in the text; no matched benign-control comparison.
statements.problem: The pooled 52.5% decrease is assigned to conversion into advice/chat format, although the medical and aesthetic interventions convert in the opposite direction.

statements.correction: Reported pooled average decrease: 52.5%; medical and aesthetic datasets reformatted into code; insecure code reformatted into advice-seeking; no isolated insecure-code effect size stated numerically.
statements.problem: Advice-seeking reformatting describes only the insecure-code intervention, not the interventions pooled into the 52.5% average.

statements.correction: Medical advice and aesthetic preferences → code; insecure code → advice-seeking; pooled average decrease across tested models and datasets: 52.5%.
statements.problem: The 52.5% average includes both code-format and advice-format rewriting; it is not a pooled estimate solely of code-format rewriting.

statements.correction: Medical advice and aesthetic preferences rewritten into code; insecure code rewritten into advice-seeking; content retained; decreases reported across tested models and datasets.
statements.problem: The description of pooled EM effectiveness should distinguish the two directions of format conversion.

statements.correction: Section 3: prompts sorted by distance and partitioned into equal-sized bins containing at most 20 prompts; mean evilness reported within bins. Across 12 settings: EM mean Spearman −0.731; base-model mean Spearman −0.067.
